0.title: The Gospel and the Slave: Paul's Letter to Philemon
0.overview:
The message. Philemon is the most personal of Paul’s surviving letters: twenty-five verses from a prisoner to a friend on behalf of a slave. There is no doctrinal argument, no church dispute, no vision of the end; just a man writing to a man about a third man. Yet the gospel is in every line. A runaway who had wronged his master has become a Christian, and Paul sends him home asking that he be received “no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother” (v. 16), with any debt charged to Paul’s own account (v. 18). That the church kept this private note among its Scriptures, and that even Marcion, a second-century teacher who threw out much of the New Testament, kept it, shows that the early church saw more here than a letter about a household matter.

Background: the writer. Paul writes with Timothy (v. 1), and calls himself not an apostle but “a prisoner for Christ Jesus” and “an old man” (vv. 1, 9). Almost no one, ancient or modern, doubts that the letter is his. He was most likely under house arrest in Rome, about AD 60–62, guarded but free to receive visitors (Acts 28:16, 30–31). This is the same imprisonment from which he wrote Colossians, which Tychicus carried with Onesimus beside him (Colossians 4:7–9), and the two letters name the same companions: Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke (vv. 23–24; Colossians 4:10–14). Some place the letter in an imprisonment at Ephesus, only about a hundred miles (160 km) from Colossae, which would make Onesimus’s journey and Paul’s hoped-for visit (v. 22) easier; others suggest Caesarea. But Rome is where Acts leaves Paul receiving all who came to him, and a runaway could hope to disappear in the capital. This commentary takes Rome as the more likely setting.

The household at Colossae. Philemon was a well-to-do believer at Colossae, in the Lycus valley of the Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Turkey. A church met in his home (v. 2), and his love had “refreshed” the hearts of the saints (v. 7). He had probably come to faith through Paul, perhaps during Paul’s years at Ephesus, when the gospel spread through the province (Acts 19:10), for Paul can say Philemon owes him “even your own self” (v. 19). Apphia was probably his wife, and Archippus, Paul’s “fellow soldier”, perhaps their son, a man with a ministry in the church (Colossians 4:17). Onesimus was one of Philemon’s slaves. Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world, a large part of the population of any city, and a slave was his master’s property in law. A runaway was counted a thief: he had stolen himself, robbing his master of his labour, and v. 18 suggests Onesimus also owed or had taken money. If caught, he could be flogged, branded or worse.

What prompted the letter. We are not told how Onesimus came to Paul. He may have been caught and imprisoned with him, or he may have sought Paul out deliberately, as a friend of his master who could plead for him, a recognised practice in Roman law. Either way, he heard the gospel from Paul and became a believer, Paul’s “child … whose father I became in my imprisonment” (v. 10). He also became a real help to Paul. Paul would gladly have kept him (v. 13), but the wrong done to Philemon had to be put right, and Paul would not act without Philemon’s consent (v. 14). So he sent Onesimus home, at real risk to him, carrying this letter, to be read before the whole church in the house (vv. 1–2). The letter’s survival is itself good evidence that Philemon did what was asked.

How the letter makes its case. The letter is a masterpiece of persuasion that still leaves Philemon free. After the greeting (vv. 1–3), Paul gives thanks for Philemon’s love and faith, and especially for how he has refreshed the saints (vv. 4–7): the very thing Paul is about to ask for. Then comes the appeal (vv. 8–16). Paul could command, but “for love’s sake I prefer to appeal to you” (vv. 8–9). He names Onesimus only after calling him “my child” (v. 10), and plays on his name, which means “useful”: “Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me” (v. 11). He is sending back “my very heart” (v. 12), and wonders whether God’s providence lay behind the parting, “that you might have him back forever” (v. 15), now as a brother “both in the flesh and in the Lord” (v. 16). Then come the terms (vv. 17–22): “receive him as you would receive me” (v. 17); any debt is Paul’s, written in his own hand (vv. 18–19); he is confident Philemon “will do even more than I say” (v. 21), perhaps a hint at freedom; and he asks for a guest room, since he hopes to come (v. 22). Greetings and a blessing close the letter (vv. 23–25). One word runs through it, splanchna, the heart (vv. 7, 12, 20): Philemon has refreshed the hearts of the saints; Onesimus is Paul’s heart; now “Refresh my heart in Christ” (v. 20).

Where it leads: to Christ. The letter acts out the gospel. A guilty runaway is received on the account of another, who says, “charge that to my account … I will repay it” (vv. 18–19). Luther said that we are all Onesimus, and the picture fits: Christ, who “knew no sin”, took our debt upon himself, “so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Corinthians 5:21), and God receives us for his sake. Paul himself had laid aside his rights to plead for another, as Christ laid aside his. And the letter shows the new family Christ makes. In him “there is neither slave nor free” (Galatians 3:28), so master and slave now share the Lord’s Table and call each other brother. Paul does not call here for the end of slavery, but he plants a truth that slavery cannot live with: the slave is his master’s brother, and that bond is meant to be lived in the actual house, not only in church. In time that truth helped bring the institution down.

For us. Philemon shows the gospel at work where it costs most, in a damaged relationship between two real people. It asks the one who was wronged to receive the one who wronged him, and the one who did wrong to go back and face it. It shows how to plead for another person with love rather than force, and what it means to treat a fellow believer of lower standing as family. And it reminds every Christian who he is: a runaway brought home, whose debt Christ has paid, and who is now called to welcome others as he has been welcomed.

1.title: Grace and a Brother: The Complete Letter
1.overview:
Where we are. Philemon is one chapter: the whole letter, from greeting to farewell, on a single page.

The message. Receive the brother who wronged you as Christ has received you. Onesimus, Philemon’s runaway slave, has become a Christian, and Paul sends him home to be welcomed “as a beloved brother” (v. 16), with any debt charged to Paul. The gospel that made Philemon a son must now make his slave his brother, in the house as well as in the church.

Why it was said. A returning runaway faced punishment in law, and a master who welcomed one home would lose face among his neighbours (see the introduction). The letter answers a question every injured Christian meets: does the grace I have received oblige me to give the same grace to the one who hurt me?

How the chapter makes its case. Paul sets down his authority from the first line, writing as “a prisoner” (vv. 1–3). He thanks God for Philemon’s love “for all the saints” and for refreshing their hearts (vv. 4–7), the very thing he is about to ask. He appeals rather than commands (vv. 8–9), presents Onesimus as his son, once useless and now useful (vv. 10–11), sends him back at real cost (vv. 12–14), and reads the episode as God’s providence giving Philemon a brother forever (vv. 15–16). The request is one sentence (v. 17); Paul signs for the debt in his own hand (vv. 18–19), expects “even more” and announces a visit (vv. 20–22). One word ties it together: splanchna, the heart (vv. 7, 12, 20).

Where it leads. The letter acts the gospel out. A guilty runaway is received on the account of another, who says, “charge that to my account … I will repay it” (vv. 18–19). Luther said we are all Onesimus: the Son of God laid aside his rights, took our debt and paid it in full, and the Father receives us as he receives his Son, making master and slave brothers at one table.

For us. Every believer is a runaway brought home at another’s cost. So we are to treat the one who wronged us, and the one of lower standing we have learned to overlook, as Christ has treated us; and the one who did wrong is to go back and face it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The greeting already does the letter’s work. Paul writes as a prisoner, not an apostle, so his rank cannot force the decision (v. 1). He names Philemon’s household and the whole church in his house, so the decision will be made before the family of God, all of whom belong to one Lord (v. 2). And he wishes them the grace and peace that the letter will ask Philemon to pass on (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Credential He Sets Down

Paul opens not with his office but with his chains, and addresses a letter about one man's slave to the whole church in that man's house.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the church in the house would all hear the letter read together.

Now: Paul makes the decision public among believers (on whether that is pressure, see the question at vv. 1–2).

verseByVerse.quote: Paul, a prisoner for Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker and Apphia our sister and Archippus our fellow soldier, and the church in your house:
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul writes as a prisoner, not an apostle, to Philemon, his household and the church that meets in his home. Before he asks anything, he has set down his rank and gathered the family of God around the decision.

A prisoner for Christ Jesus. Paul does not call himself an apostle here. About to ask a slave owner to do something extraordinary, he sets aside the one title that could have forced him to do it. Everything in this letter is designed to leave Philemon free.

And Timothy our brother. A second name on a private letter about a domestic matter: Philemon will know that Timothy has read it too.

To Philemon our beloved fellow worker. Philemon had worked with Paul in the gospel, perhaps by hosting the church, and had probably come to faith through him (v. 19; see the introduction).

And Apphia our sister. Probably Philemon’s wife, who would have managed the slaves day to day. Paul names her as a sister, a member of the family Onesimus has just joined.

And Archippus our fellow soldier. Perhaps their son, and a minister in the church, the man told in Colossians 4:17 to fulfil the ministry he had received.

And the church in your house. The early churches met in homes (Romans 16:5). A letter about one man’s slave goes to the whole congregation that meets in his living room, and they will watch what he does next. It travelled with Colossians, and Onesimus came with its bearer (Colossians 4:7–9).

Bound before Paul was. The Lord Jesus became a prisoner for us before Paul was ever a prisoner for him. He was bound in a garden, led from court to court, and laid aside all his rights, so that runaways could be brought home.

Christ is all, and in all. This letter puts to the test a sentence the same house church would hear in Colossians: “Here there is not Greek and Jew, circumcised and uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, free; but Christ is all, and in all” (3:11). What gathers in Philemon’s living room is not the master’s family with his slaves at the back, but people who all belong to the same Lord.

Isn’t addressing the whole church a kind of pressure? Yes, but look at the kind of pressure. Paul does not command, threaten or invoke his office; he makes the decision public, among brothers, and trusts what the gospel has already done in this house. Manipulation hides its aims and works on fear; honest appeal says openly what it wants and leaves the other person free. In a church, how a believer treats someone who has wronged him is not only his own business; it shows the family what the gospel is.
verseByVerse.note: Philemon was a well-to-do believer at Colossae whose home hosted the church. Apphia may have been his wife and Archippus his son. Paul wrote from prison, sending this letter with Colossians.

verseByVerse.quote: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul wishes the church the grace and peace that come from God the Father and the Lord Jesus, the very grace he is about to ask Philemon to pass on.

Grace to you and peace. The letter is bracketed by grace (v. 25), and the question it puts is whether a man whom God has treated with grace can treat someone else the same way. Peace is things put right, a pointed word to open a letter about a broken household.

From God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. “You” is plural: Paul is still speaking to the room. One word will do quiet work all the way through: Lord. Kyrios is the ordinary Greek for master, the word a slave used of his owner. Philemon is Onesimus’s kyrios, but Paul names a Lord above them both, and by the end he will ask Philemon to receive his slave as a brother, because they now have the same Lord.

How do I show grace to someone who has wronged me, when I do not feel gracious? Start where Paul starts: with the grace you have received. You do not manufacture grace out of your own reserves; you pass on what has been given to you, and you have been given more than you will ever have to give (Ephesians 4:32; Matthew 18:21–35). Feelings often follow obedience. So pray for the person, refuse to rehearse the wrong, speak kindly, and take one concrete step toward peace. Grace does not pretend the wrong did not happen, nor require you to trust someone who has not changed; but it lets go of the right to pay them back.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Paul’s thanksgiving is sincere, and it also lays the ground for the request. He thanks God for Philemon’s faith in the Lord Jesus and his love for “all the saints” (vv. 4–5), prays that the fellowship this faith creates will become active (v. 6), and rejoices that Philemon has refreshed the hearts of the saints (v. 7). That known love is about to meet a saint Philemon had not counted.
verseByVerse.theology:
An Argument Built from a Man's Own Character

Paul tells Philemon what he already is, and asks him to be it consistently (see vv. 4–5). The words that describe Philemon's reputation in verse 7 come back in verses 12 and 20 (see the note on vv. 6–7).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Philemon was known for his love 'for all the saints'.

Now: When you must ask something hard of another Christian, name the grace already at work in them and ask them to extend it to the case they had left out.

verseByVerse.quote: I thank my God always when I remember you in my prayers, because I hear of your love and of the faith that you have toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints,
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul thanks God for Philemon’s faith in the Lord Jesus and his love for all the saints. He describes the man truthfully, and the word “all” will soon have to stretch to include Onesimus.

I thank my God always. “You” is singular from here until verse 22: Paul now addresses Philemon personally.

Because I hear. Reports kept coming, perhaps from Epaphras (v. 23) or Onesimus himself. Love comes first, perhaps deliberately, since it is love that Paul will appeal to (v. 9).

Toward the Lord Jesus and for all the saints. The words pair crosswise: faith toward the Lord Jesus, love for all the saints. “All” is the word the whole letter turns on: every believer, including, now, Philemon’s own runaway slave.

Faith and love belong together. Paul learned that on the Damascus road, when the risen Jesus asked him, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). To harm Christ’s people was to harm Christ; and love for the saints is faith in Christ taking hold of the people he has made his own. So Philemon will not be asked to love a new category of person, only to see that the Lord he trusts has already claimed this one.

The method of the letter. Paul does not begin with what Philemon ought to be, but with what he truthfully already is, and then asks him to be it consistently, which is harder to refuse than a rebuke and treats him as an adult rather than a problem. If you must raise something difficult with someone, begin, honestly and specifically, with what you see of God’s grace in them.

How do I love all the saints, including Christians I find difficult? Remember that the word is all, and that you love them not because they are easy but because Christ loved them. Start with prayer: it is very hard to keep resenting someone you pray for by name. Then act before you feel: greet them, ask how they are, do them a kindness. Look for grace in them and thank God for it, as Paul did. And notice whom you have, without meaning to, left out of your all: the new, the awkward, the poor, those from a different background. Onesimus was one of those.

verseByVerse.quote: and I pray that the sharing of your faith may become effective for the full knowledge of every good thing that is in us for the sake of Christ. For I have derived much joy and comfort from your love, my brother, because the hearts of the saints have been refreshed through you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul prays that the fellowship Philemon’s faith has created will become active, as he comes to know all the good that is his in Christ; and he rejoices that Philemon has already given rest to the hearts of the saints. He is praying, in advance, for the very thing he is about to ask.

The sharing of your faith. “Sharing” is koinōnia: fellowship, partnership, having in common. It prepares for v. 17: “if you consider me your partner”.

May become effective. The Greek gives us our word energy: Paul prays that this fellowship will actually do something, and the next paragraph brings the case.

The hearts of the saints have been refreshed. “Hearts” (splanchna) is literally the inward parts, the seat of deep feeling; “refreshed” means given rest, as for a tired traveller. Watch these two words. In v. 12 Onesimus is Paul’s splanchna, “my very heart”; in v. 20 Paul asks Philemon to refresh his heart, by receiving Onesimus. He is building his case out of Philemon’s own character.

Fellowship that begins with the Son. The partnership Paul prays for has its source in a deeper one: “God is faithful, by whom you were called into the fellowship of his Son, Jesus Christ our Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:9). Believers share a life with one another because each first shares in Christ: his death, his righteousness, his Spirit, his inheritance. That is “every good thing that is in us”. A man who sees how much he has been given in Christ finds it far easier to give a runaway what he does not deserve.

The great refresher of weary hearts. “Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). Jesus gives rest still, often through his people: every hot meal set before an exhausted parent, every evening of company for a lonely widow, is his rest passing from one heart to another, a foretaste of the Sabbath rest that remains for the people of God (Hebrews 4:9).

How do I refresh the hearts of the saints? It is ordinary work, open to any believer. Notice who is tired. The weary rarely announce it; ask how someone really is, and wait for the answer. Lighten a load someone is carrying alone. Name the grace you see. Tell a brother or sister specifically where you have seen God at work in them, as Paul does here. Open your door. The church met in Philemon’s house (v. 2), and an open table is still one of the quickest ways to give rest. You can only pass on rest you have first received, and Philemon’s came from Christ, who gave himself so that weary sinners could stop carrying their own guilt. Keep going back to him, and his rest will keep reaching others through you.

Uncertain wording. Verse 6 is often called the hardest sentence in the letter to translate: the Greek is compressed, and it is not certain how “sharing”, “effective”, “full knowledge” and “for the sake of Christ” connect. The King James Version’s “the communication of thy faith” led many to read it as a prayer for Philemon’s witness to unbelievers. But the word means fellowship or partnership, and the more likely sense is that Paul prays for the generous fellowship that flows from Philemon’s faith to bear fruit as he grows in knowing all the good that is ours in Christ: exactly what he is about to ask of him. Evangelism is commanded elsewhere (Matthew 28:19–20; 1 Peter 3:15); this verse is about the common life believers share.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Here the letter turns from thanks to appeal, and reaches the sentence it exists to deliver: a slave is now a brother. Paul sets aside the authority he could use and pleads in love (vv. 8–9). He introduces the runaway as his own son, changed by grace (vv. 10–11), and sends him back though it costs him his heart, because goodness must be freely given (vv. 12–14). Then he asks Philemon to see God’s hand in the parting: he lost a slave for a while to gain a brother forever, in daily life as well as in the Lord (vv. 15–16).
verseByVerse.theology:
Goodness by Compulsion Is Not Goodness

Verse 14 governs the letter: Paul wants Philemon's goodness to be 'of your own accord'. Verse 16 is its heart: a beloved brother, 'both in the flesh and in the Lord'.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: A runaway slave met Paul in prison and was sent home as a brother.

Now: There is a real difference between the pressure of authority and the pressure of affection, and only one of them leaves a man free.

verseByVerse.quote: Accordingly, though I am bold enough in Christ to command you to do what is required, yet for love's sake I prefer to appeal to you—I, Paul, an old man and now a prisoner also for Christ Jesus—
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul has the authority to command Philemon, but he chooses to appeal to him in love, as an old man in chains.

Bold enough in Christ to command you. As an apostle Paul could give orders. He names that authority in plain view, so Philemon sees exactly what is being set down: the opposite of manipulation.

What is required. Receiving Onesimus well is not optional. What Philemon should do is not in doubt; the question is whether he will do it freely.

For love’s sake. Either Philemon’s love or the love that binds believers. A command can produce obedience; only an appeal can produce a willing heart, and v. 14 says why that matters: goodness that is forced is not really goodness.

An old man and now a prisoner also. Paul was probably around sixty, worn by beatings, shipwrecks and prison, and he openly leans on his age and his chains. The pressure of affection, unlike the pressure of authority, leaves a man free. Paul spent his life insisting on his apostleship when the gospel was at stake; here, where only a slave’s future is at stake, he lays it down without a murmur.

Lord and Teacher, with a towel. The night before he died, Jesus washed his disciples’ feet and then said, “You call me Teacher and Lord, and you are right, for so I am” (John 13:13). He named his authority, and used it to kneel. Paul, appealing as an old man in chains, is following his Master, and asking Philemon to do the same: to use his rights as a master to stoop to a slave.

Yet over and over he pleads. God has every right to command; yet over and over he pleads: “Come now, let us reason together” (Isaiah 1:18); “we implore you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Corinthians 5:20). The Lord of glory stands at the door and knocks (Revelation 3:20). He wins his people by love, until they offer themselves freely in the day of his power (Psalm 110:3), and the yes he receives is the free yes he wanted all along.

When should a parent, leader or elder command rather than appeal? When the matter is clear, urgent or dangerous, or when appeal has been refused: a child running into the road needs an order, not an invitation, and Paul gave firm commands where the gospel or the church’s purity was at stake (2 Thessalonians 3:6; 1 Corinthians 5). But wherever you can, appeal: explain why, show what love and the gospel ask, and let them choose. That grows mature believers rather than compliant ones. Authority that is always used is soon resented; authority held in reserve and laid down in love is rarely needed.

Uncertain wording. The word translated “an old man” (presbytēs) was sometimes written for “ambassador” (presbeutēs), and some scholars read “ambassador” here (compare Ephesians 6:20, “an ambassador in chains”). Both fit Paul, but “old man” is the plain meaning of the word as written and suits an appeal that deliberately sets authority aside; this commentary follows it.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeal to you for my child, Onesimus, whose father I became in my imprisonment. (Formerly he was useless to you, but now he is indeed useful to you and to me.)
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul pleads for Onesimus as his own son in the faith, and admits that the slave who was useless to Philemon has, through conversion, become what his name means: useful.

For my child. In the Greek the appeal and the relationship come before the name, so by the time Philemon hears it, Paul has already claimed the runaway as a son.

Onesimus. The name means useful or profitable, a common slave name, given for the obvious reason (see Onesimus).

Whose father I became in my imprisonment. Paul led him to Christ while in chains, and uses the language of spiritual fatherhood (1 Corinthians 4:15; Galatians 4:19). The runaway had gone to the obvious place to disappear and there met the one man in the empire most likely to send him home. God used Paul’s chains and Onesimus’s flight to save him.

Formerly he was useless to you. Useful was useless (achrēston), possibly with a play on Christos too, since a-chrēstos may have sounded like “without Christ”. The joke is gentle, and it is an admission: Paul does not pretend the man was a good servant badly treated, and v. 18 allows that he owes money besides. He concedes the whole charge.

But now he is indeed useful. The word (euchrēston) may have sounded like “good Christ”. Conversion has made him what his name said. Grace does not only forgive a man’s past; it makes him worth something (2 Timothy 2:21; 4:11, where the same word is used of Mark).

Useful because he is in Christ. “If anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation” (2 Corinthians 5:17). The Lord who “came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45) now lived in a household slave, and the faithfulness Paul found in him was Christ’s own life taking shape in a runaway.

He follows runaways down every road. We were all once achrēstos, without Christ and of no use to God, and none of us went looking for him. He came after us: “the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost” (Luke 19:10). He follows runaways down every road until he finds them, often in the last place they expected, and makes them his children, with a name and a usefulness they could never have earned. A slave who ran from his master ran straight into the arms of his Lord.

How do I know whether someone who wronged me has really changed? Look for the fruit Paul could point to. Onesimus did not merely say sorry: he came back to face the man he had wronged, did not hide the debt, and had proved himself in service over time. Real repentance owns the wrong without excuses, puts right what can be put right, and shows itself in lasting change (Luke 19:8; 2 Corinthians 7:11). Forgiveness can be given at once; trust is rebuilt over time. You may forgive fully and still wait, wisely, to see the fruit before handing back responsibility.
verseByVerse.note: Onesimus was Philemon’s slave who had run away. His name means “useful,” and Paul plays on it.

verseByVerse.quote: I am sending him back to you, sending my very heart. I would have been glad to keep him with me, in order that he might serve me on your behalf during my imprisonment for the gospel, but I preferred to do nothing without your consent in order that your goodness might not be by compulsion but of your own accord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul sends Onesimus home, though it costs him his own heart, because he will not keep what belongs to Philemon without his consent: goodness must be freely given. The appeal is made after the risk has already been taken.

I am sending him back to you. Paul does not hide Onesimus, or argue that conversion has cancelled the legal position. He puts him on the road to Colossae with a letter in his hand. A returning fugitive could be branded, flogged or worse (see slavery), and both men knew it. Onesimus showed courage and repentance in going.

Sending my very heart. The word of v. 7 (splanchna): Philemon refreshes the hearts of the saints, and Paul is sending him his own. The Father did it first: he sent his Son, his very heart, into a hostile world, knowing what it would cost.

I would have been glad to keep him with me. Paul says so plainly: returning him was not easy.

On your behalf. Paul tactfully treats the help Onesimus gave him as Philemon’s own gift, the service Philemon would gladly have given in person, and hints that Philemon might send him back.

Not by compulsion but of your own accord. This sentence governs the whole letter. Paul could have kept Onesimus, or written a letter Philemon could not refuse. He did neither, because a good deed done under compulsion looks like goodness and is empty inside (2 Corinthians 9:7). God deals with us the same way. He does not force the will; when he saves, he renews it, giving a new heart that wants what he wants (Ezekiel 36:26; Philippians 2:13).

Freely, as he gave himself. Nobody compelled the Son of God: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord” (John 10:18), the very phrase Paul uses of Philemon’s goodness. He “loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20). The fitting answer to a gospel of free grace is a glad and free response, so what Paul wants from Philemon is what Christ gave Philemon: goodness entirely of its own accord.

Should a new Christian go back and face the consequences of past wrongs? Often, yes. Conversion cancels guilt before God, not just obligations to people. Zacchaeus repaid what he had taken (Luke 19:8); Onesimus went back. A believer who has stolen should repay where he can; one who has committed a crime may need to confess it to the authorities; one who has wronged a family member should seek them out. Do it wisely, with counsel from your pastor, especially where there are legal implications or where contact might harm the person wronged. The aim is not to earn forgiveness, which Christ has won, but to walk in the light.

Did not the law forbid returning a runaway slave to his master? Deuteronomy 23:15–16 forbade Israel to hand back a slave who had escaped to them from his master in another land. Paul is sending a brother back to a fellow believer, with a letter asking that he be received as Paul himself (v. 17): to a changed household, not to punishment. Sadly, slaveholders in later centuries cited this letter to justify returning fugitive slaves, ignoring everything it actually asks.

verseByVerse.quote: For this perhaps is why he was parted from you for a while, that you might have him back forever, no longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother—especially to me, but how much more to you, both in the flesh and in the Lord.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul suggests that God may have been at work in Onesimus’s flight, parting him from Philemon for a while so that he could be given back forever, no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother, in daily life as well as in the Lord.

For this perhaps is why. Paul claims no certain knowledge; he offers Philemon a way of reading his loss. He does not say “he ran away” but “he was parted from you”, hinting at God’s hidden hand. Joseph spoke as gently to his brothers: “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). Providence works even through human sin, without excusing it.

For a while … back forever. “For a while” is literally for an hour, set against forever: a few months of loss against an eternity of brotherhood. Paul asks Philemon to do the arithmetic.

More than a bondservant, as a beloved brother. Paul does not order Onesimus’s release. He says something that in the long run does more to undo slavery: whatever his legal status, Onesimus is no longer to be thought of first as a slave. Philemon may still hold the papers, but he may no longer look at him and see property. He must see a brother, an equal member of God’s family (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11), who will sit beside him at the Lord’s Table now and in the life to come.

Both in the flesh and in the Lord. In the actual house and the daily arrangements, not merely in a spiritual realm where equality costs nothing. Paul will not let the brotherhood be confined to Sunday.

Brothers because of the firstborn. A brotherhood strong enough to outlast slavery comes from the Son. Christ is “the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29), and “he is not ashamed to call them brothers” (Hebrews 2:11). Onesimus and Philemon became brothers the day each became Christ’s, and it is forever because it rests not on Roman law but on Christ, who will never disown either of them. To refuse Onesimus as a brother would be to refuse the relationship on which Philemon’s own salvation rested.

Connections we can delete. Onesimus dealt with a difficult relationship the way people always have: he left. Our age makes leaving easier than ever. The sociologist Zygmunt Bauman, in Liquid Love (2003), argued that modern people prefer connections to relationships, because a connection can be ended at the press of a button. That feels like freedom, and it is part of why so many are lonely: nobody can be deeply known by people who are always free to leave. Paul sends the runaway back into a bond that cannot be deleted: “forever”. That is possible only because of the one relationship that was never liquid. Christ did not walk away from those who wronged him; he came back for them, all the way to the cross. A brother like that makes it possible to go back and face your Philemon.

In everyday life. Pick one person whose relationship to you is defined mostly by role: the cleaner, the employee, the carer. If they are a believer, they are your brother or sister forever; if not, they bear God’s image. Treat them that way this week, by name.

How should I read God’s providence in my own losses? With Paul’s perhaps. You may be sure that God works all things for good for those who love him (Romans 8:28), and you may sometimes see, looking back, what he was doing. But you will not always see it, and you must never use providence to excuse a wrong. Joseph’s brothers were still guilty; Onesimus still owed his master. The sin was real, and God was not absent from it. And be slow to explain others’ suffering to them: offer a perhaps, gently, only if it comforts.

Does the Bible, then, condone slavery? No. Paul’s silence about abolition is not approval, though it is honest to admit that the New Testament regulates slavery rather than forbidding it outright, and that this troubles many readers. Paul worked in a society where slavery was everywhere and could not be changed by a letter, but he planted what would destroy it: a slave is a beloved brother; slaves should gain their freedom if they can (1 Corinthians 7:21, on the most likely reading of a verse some translate differently); and enslavers are listed among the lawless (1 Timothy 1:10). Roman slavery was also not the race-based chattel slavery of later centuries, which began with man-stealing, a crime the law of Moses punished with death (Exodus 21:16).

How the gospel undid it. The gospel did not overthrow slavery by decree; it set beside it a truth a slave society could not survive being told: the man in the kitchen is your brother, in the house as well as in the assembly. Many Christians took centuries to see that they could not hold it while owning their brothers, but Christian abolitionists drew on exactly these truths, and where they were believed, the institution became unthinkable.

Where Christians differ: did Paul want Onesimus freed? Some think he was silently content for Onesimus to remain a slave; others think he was hinting strongly at freedom. This commentary’s view: Paul does not explicitly demand freedom, but “no longer as a bondservant,” “more than a bondservant,” “receive him as you would receive me” (v. 17), and “you will do even more than I say” (v. 21) all point strongly that way. Early tradition suggests an Onesimus later became bishop of Ephesus; if this is the same man, Philemon presumably freed him. More importantly, Paul establishes the principle of brotherhood that makes slavery incompatible with the gospel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 17–25 — Receive Him as You Would Receive Me
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The request is one sentence long: receive Onesimus as you would receive Paul (v. 17). Paul backs it with his own signature on the debt, a picture of the gospel itself (vv. 18–19). He asks Philemon to refresh his heart, trusts him to do even more than he says, and announces a visit that will let him see the welcome for himself (vv. 20–22). The letter closes with greetings from Paul’s companions and the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ (vv. 23–25).
verseByVerse.theology:
Charge That to My Account

Verses 17-19 act out the gospel instead of explaining it: a debt is taken on by another, in writing, and the debtor is to be received 'as you would receive me'.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Welcoming a runaway slave to his table would cost Philemon standing among the slave-owning households of Colossae.

Now: Paul asks for more than private forgiveness and then promises to come and see (v. 22). Reconciliation that must be explained face to face is harder to leave half-done.

verseByVerse.quote: So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the request: Philemon is to welcome Onesimus as he would welcome Paul himself. Not merely to forgive him or take him back, but to give him the welcome an apostle and old friend would be given at the door.

So if you consider me your partner. “Partner” is related to the “sharing” of v. 6, and the “if” expresses no doubt: “since you do”. Paul is not asking whether Philemon will obey an apostle, but what a partnership is worth when it becomes expensive.

Receive him as you would receive me. “Receive” is the word Paul uses of how Christ received us: “welcome one another as Christ has welcomed you” (Romans 15:7).

What it would cost. A runaway is to be welcomed as the most honoured guest the house could receive. Philemon’s other slaves will be watching, and slave-owning neighbours will hear; a master who welcomes a runaway to his table would seem to have lost control of his house. For a man like Philemon the idol was less likely to be money than standing. The gospel does not flatter that. It asks him to lose face for a brother, as Christ “emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant” for us (Philippians 2:7), and the Spirit of that Christ, at work in him, makes such a stoop possible.

The deeper pattern. The offender is received because of the one who speaks for him, and is given that person’s welcome. That is how Philemon himself was accepted: God has “blessed us in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6), and the Father receives us as he receives his Son. We came to the Father’s door as runaways, with nothing to offer and a debt behind us, and the Son stood beside us and said, “receive him as you would receive me”.

Does receiving a repentant person mean ignoring past harm? No. Receiving is welcome, not amnesia; Onesimus’s debt was faced, not denied (v. 18). In a church, a repentant brother is welcomed back to fellowship, to the Lord’s Table and to friendship. But where the wrong involved abuse, violence or danger to others, love for the vulnerable still governs: the church must report crimes to the authorities, protect those at risk, and may rightly limit where and how the person serves, however sincere his repentance. Forgiveness restores a brother to the family; it does not require placing him where he could harm someone again. Abuse is never to be tolerated or hidden in the name of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything, charge that to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand: I will repay it—to say nothing of your owing me even your own self.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul takes whatever Onesimus owes onto his own account, in writing, and gently reminds Philemon that he owes Paul far more.

If he has wronged you at all, or owes you anything. The “if” is most likely a courtesy: a runaway could hardly travel far without money, and his absence had cost Philemon his labour. Paul concedes the wrong without dwelling on it.

Charge that to my account. An accounting term: put it on my ledger. Paul is not asking Philemon to absorb the loss; he is offering to pay.

I, Paul, write this with my own hand. Whether he took the pen from his secretary here or wrote the whole letter, this line is a binding IOU, in a letter the whole church will hear.

To say nothing of your owing me even your own self. The lightest touch in the letter: Paul mentions, while saying he will not, that Philemon, probably converted through him, owes him everything. It is done with a smile, and it is unanswerable. What is a household debt against a man’s own soul?

We are all Onesimus. Luther wrote that we are all Onesimuses: as Paul took on Onesimus’s debt so that Philemon would receive him, so Christ took on our debt so that the Father would receive us. The whole gospel is here: a man with a debt he cannot pay; another who takes it on himself in writing, at his own cost; and the wronged party asked to receive the debtor as though he were the one who paid. Paul has spent his letters teaching this; here he simply does it, for a single man.

He took the debt as his own. The Son of God looked at a debt no sinner could pay and paid it in full with his own blood, “canceling the record of debt that stood against us with its legal demands. This he set aside, nailing it to the cross” (Colossians 2:14): a sentence written to the very town where Philemon kept his accounts. And we, who owe him our very selves, are not sent a bill. We are received as sons.

What does it mean that my debt was charged to Christ? Every sin you have committed, against God and against others, was entered on Christ’s account and paid in full at the cross (Isaiah 53:5–6; Colossians 2:13–14). God did not pretend your debt away; he transferred it to his Son, who bore its whole penalty, and credited Christ’s perfect obedience to you, so that he receives you as righteous (2 Corinthians 5:21; Romans 5:19). That is why a believer can have peace with God even on his worst day. The account is settled not by your improvement but by his payment, and settled forever.

Does forgiving someone mean cancelling every debt and every consequence? Forgiveness gives up the right to take revenge and to hold the wrong against the person; it does not always make every practical debt disappear. Paul does not pretend the money is not owed; he arranges for it to be paid. Sometimes love will cancel a debt outright, as Philemon perhaps did; sometimes repayment is right and good for the one who did wrong; and where the law has been broken, the courts may still have their say (Romans 13:4). What forgiveness forbids is bitterness, grudge-keeping and personal vengeance.
verseByVerse.note: Paul probably led Philemon to Christ, perhaps during his years at Ephesus.

verseByVerse.quote: Yes, brother, I want some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say. At the same time, prepare a guest room for me, for I am hoping that through your prayers I will be graciously given to you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul asks Philemon to refresh his heart by welcoming Onesimus, trusts him to do even more than he asks, and announces that he hopes to come and stay.

Yes, brother, I want some benefit from you. “Brother” is the very word Paul has asked Philemon to use of Onesimus (v. 16). “Benefit” (onaimēn) shares a root with Onesimus: let me have some Onesimus from you.

Refresh my heart in Christ. The two words of v. 7 again: since Onesimus is Paul’s very heart (v. 12), refreshing Onesimus refreshes Paul. He asks for the thing this man is famous for, in the one case where it will cost him. And twice, “in the Lord” and “in Christ”, he reminds Philemon that all this is between people who belong to Christ.

Confident of your obedience. Though Paul appealed rather than commanded (vv. 8–9), he still expects obedience, finally not to himself but to the Lord who had made Philemon what he was and who will carry on the good work he began in him (Philippians 1:6).

Even more than I say. What could be more than receiving Onesimus as a brother? The obvious candidate is freedom, and perhaps sending him back to serve Paul in the gospel. Paul leaves the door open without walking through it, because naming it would make it a command and destroy what v. 14 insisted on: goodness freely given.

Prepare a guest room for me. Paul hopes to be released and to visit: the gentlest pressure, said warmly, and unmistakably a way of holding Philemon to account. A decision you will have to explain to someone’s face is different from one made at a distance.

Through your prayers I will be graciously given to you. “Your” is plural: the whole church’s prayers. Paul believes prayer matters to his release, though the outcome is God’s gift of grace.

God always does more than he says. He promised a seed to Abraham and gave him a multitude; he promised forgiveness and gave adoption, an inheritance and the Spirit. He “is able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think” (Ephesians 3:20). The “even more” Paul hoped for from Philemon is a small human echo of the even more that runs through everything God gives.

In everyday life. If you have forgiven someone, look for the extra step: the invitation, the gift, the public word of welcome that makes the forgiveness visible.

Was Paul released, and did he visit? He expected to be (compare Philippians 1:25), and the early church believed he was released from his first Roman imprisonment and travelled again before his final arrest; the Pastoral Letters fit that picture (1 Timothy 1:3; Titus 1:5; 2 Timothy 4:13, 20). Whether he reached Colossae, Scripture does not say; but he expected a small house church’s prayers to be part of how God would answer.
verseByVerse.note: “Benefit” (onaimēn) plays once more on the name Onesimus, “useful.”

verseByVerse.quote: Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends greetings to you, and so do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Paul closes with greetings from the same companions who greet the Colossians, and with the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ on the whole church. The letter ends where it began, in grace.

Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus. The five names are the circle that closes Colossians (Colossians 4:10–14), one reason the two letters are thought to have travelled together. Epaphras founded the church at Colossae (Colossians 1:7); he was perhaps literally imprisoned with Paul, or voluntarily sharing his confinement.

Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. Mark, who had turned back from the mission (Acts 13:13; 15:38), now restored (2 Timothy 4:11). Aristarchus, who had suffered with Paul (Acts 19:29; 27:2). Demas, still faithful here, who would later desert Paul for love of this world (2 Timothy 4:10). Luke, the beloved physician (Colossians 4:14), who would later be the only one with him (2 Timothy 4:11). Mark was restored; Demas would fall. Faithfulness today does not guarantee faithfulness tomorrow, except by grace.

The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. “Your” is plural: everyone in that room. Paul defined this grace elsewhere: “though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich” (2 Corinthians 8:9). The letter begins (v. 3) and ends with it, and has asked throughout that a man made rich by another’s poverty should spend something of himself to receive somebody else the same way. And grace will close the story of every one of his people: received on another’s account, debts paid, brothers forever, home at last.

What happened? We are never told what Philemon did, but a letter recording a refused request would hardly have been copied and treasured by the church that heard it read. There is a further hint, no more. Some fifty years later Ignatius of Antioch wrote to the church at Ephesus in warm praise of their bishop, a man named Onesimus, and played on the name with the very verb of v. 20: may I have joy of you (onaimēn). Whether it is the same man cannot be proved, and the name was common. But it is a pleasant thought that the runaway ended his life as a bishop, and that the letter asking for his welcome was kept safe by the churches he served.

Could I fall away like Demas? Demas is a warning that outward service, even at an apostle’s side, does not prove a heart that will endure. Those who finally abandon Christ show that they were never truly his (1 John 2:19). But a true believer will be kept: the Lord who began a good work will complete it (Philippians 1:6), and he keeps us through warnings like this one, which drive us back to him. So do not presume, and do not despair. If you fear falling, that fear is itself a sign of life; take it to Christ, guard against love for this present world, stay close to his people, and lean on his grace, which held Mark after his failure and can hold you.
verseByVerse.note: The same companions greet the Colossians.

keyVerse.quote: So if you consider me your partner, receive him as you would receive me.
keyVerse.note: This is the one sentence the whole letter exists to ask, and everything before it builds towards it. A runaway is to be given the welcome due to the one who speaks for him, which is exactly how every believer has been received by the Father for Christ’s sake. The next verses show what it costs: the one who pleads also pays (vv. 18–19).

1.reflection:
Paul could have commanded Philemon but chose to appeal “for love’s sake” and leave him free (vv. 8–9, 14). Why does he care so much that Philemon’s goodness be “of your own accord”? Where do you need to appeal rather than command, at home, at work or in the church?

Philemon is asked to receive the man who wronged him “as you would receive me” (v. 17), and Onesimus to go back and face the man he wronged. Which of the two would you find harder? Is there a relationship in your life where one of these steps is waiting to be taken?

Onesimus is now Philemon’s brother “both in the flesh and in the Lord” (v. 16). Whom in your church or daily life do you tend to see mainly by their role or standing? What would it look like to treat them as family in ordinary life, not only on Sunday?

“Charge that to my account” (v. 18). Luther said we are all Onesimus. How does knowing that Christ has taken your whole debt as his own change the way you come to God, and the way you treat those who owe you?
